definition: The American National Corpus (ANC) is a text corpus of American English containing 22 million words of written and spoken data produced since 1990.
details: Currently, the ANC includes a range of genres, including emerging genres such as email, tweets, and web data that are not included in earlier corpora such as the British National Corpus. It is annotated for part of speech and lemma, shallow parse, and named entities. The ANC is available from the Linguistic Data Consortium. A fifteen million word subset of the corpus, called the Open American National Corpus (OANC), is freely available with no restrictions on its use from the ANC Website. The corpus and its annotations are provided according to the specifications of ISO/TC 37 SC4's Linguistic Annotation Framework. By using a freely provided transduction tool (ANC2Go), the corpus and user-chosen annotations are provided in multiple formats, including CoNLL IOB format, the XML format conformant to the XML Corpus Encoding Standard (XCES) (usable with the British National Corpus's XAIRA search engine), a UIMA-compliant format, and formats suitable for input to a wide variety of concordance software. Plugins to import the annotations into General Architecture for Text Engineering (GATE) are also available. The ANC differs from other corpora of English because it is richly annotated, including different part of speech annotations (Penn tags, CLAWS5 and CLAWS7 tags), shallow parse annotations, and annotations for several types of named entities. Additional annotations are added to all or parts of the corpus as they become available, often by contributions from other projects. Unlike on-line searchable corpora, which due to copyright restrictions allow access only to individual sentences, the entire ANC is available to enable research involving, for example, development of statistical language models and full-text linguistic annotation. ANC annotations are automatically produced and unvalidated. A 500,000 word subset called the Manually Annotated Sub-Corpus (MASC) is annotated for approximately 20 different kinds of linguistic annotations, all of which have been hand-validated or manually produced. These include Penn Treebank syntactic annotation, WordNet sense annotation, FrameNet semantic frame annotations, among others. Like the OANC, MASC is freely available for any use, and can be downloaded from the ANC site or from the Linguistic Data Consortium. It is also distributed in part-of-speech tagged form with the Natural Language Toolkit. The ANC and its sub-corpora differ from similar corpora primarily in the range of linguistic annotations provided and the inclusion of modern genres that do not appear in resources like the British National Corpus. Also, because the initial target use of the corpora was the development of statistical language models, the full data and all annotations are available, thus differing from the Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA) which is available only selectively through a web browser. Continued growth of the OANC and MASC relies on contributions of data and annotations from the computational linguistics and corpus linguistics communities.

explainer.lead: The American National Corpus is a large collection of written and spoken American English produced since 1990, supplied with linguistic labels such as parts of speech and named entities. It gives researchers complete text and annotations for work such as statistical language modelling, rather than limiting them to sentences viewed through a search page.

tiers.eli5: Think of it as a huge library of American English, containing 22 million words from writing and speech. Many words and passages come with labels explaining their grammar or naming people, places, and other things. A 15-million-word part and a smaller, carefully checked part are free for anyone to use.
tiers.practitioner: Use the full ANC through the Linguistic Data Consortium, or download the unrestricted 15-million-word OANC and 500,000-word MASC subsets. ANC2Go can export selected annotations as CoNLL IOB, XCES XML, UIMA-compliant data, or concordance-ready formats; GATE import plugins are available, and NLTK distributes MASC in part-of-speech-tagged form. Treat the main ANC annotations as automatic and unvalidated, and use MASC when hand-produced or hand-validated annotations are important.
tiers.paperLevel: The ANC is a 22-million-word corpus of post-1990 written and spoken American English, with part-of-speech and lemma, shallow-parse, and named-entity annotations represented under ISO/TC 37 SC4's Linguistic Annotation Framework. Its principal subsets are the unrestricted 15-million-word OANC and the 500,000-word MASC, which contains approximately 20 hand-validated or manually produced annotation types. A central limitation is that the main corpus annotations are automatically produced and unvalidated; continued growth of OANC and MASC depends on community contributions.

explainer.example: For a named-entity project, a researcher could download the 15-million-word OANC and use ANC2Go to export the text with chosen annotations in CoNLL IOB format. They could then use the 500,000-word MASC subset when they need annotations that have been manually produced or hand-validated.

usedIn.detail: Plugins import ANC annotations into the General Architecture for Text Engineering.

explainer.measures: The ANC does not score systems or people; it supplies American English text and linguistic annotations for corpus research and model development. Its scale is measured in words, with 22 million in the full corpus, 15 million in OANC, and 500,000 in MASC.
howScored: Corpus size is reported as a word count.
Written and spoken material dates from 1990 onward.
MASC annotations are manually produced or hand-validated.
explainer.formula: There is no scoring formula. In plain-text size notation: |ANC| = 22 million words, |OANC| = 15 million words, and |MASC| = 500,000 words.
explainer.typicalResults: A typical output is a full-text dataset with selected linguistic annotations in a chosen interchange format, not a numerical result. Available annotations include Penn, CLAWS5, and CLAWS7 part-of-speech tags, shallow parses, and several named-entity types.
caveats: Main ANC annotations are automatic and unvalidated.
MASC is much smaller than the full corpus.
The data represents American English produced since 1990.
OANC and MASC growth depends on contributed data and annotations.
The full ANC is obtained through the Linguistic Data Consortium.
